title: MBrain: A Multi-channel Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Brain Signals

problem.claim: Brain-signal modeling needs methods that can use data effectively despite the high cost of clinical labels and differences between invasive and non-invasive measurements.

gap.claim: Existing studies predominantly use supervised learning and lack a unified method applicable to both SEEG and EEG signals.

contributions.claim: MBrain is a self-supervised learning framework for pre-training either SEEG or EEG data.

MBrain learns implicit spatial and temporal correlations across channels using multi-channel CPC, instantaneous-time-shift prediction, delayed-time-shift prediction, and replace-discriminative learning.
The paper provides a theoretical proof relating optimization of multi-channel CPC to better predictive representations.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on seizure detection using large-scale real-world EEG and SEEG datasets reportedly show that MBrain outperforms several state-of-the-art time-series self-supervised and unsupervised models.
The authors report that the model has the ability to be deployed to clinical practice.

narrative_sequence.summary: Brain signals are important for understanding brain physiology and disease, while deep learning creates opportunities for improved modeling.
Supervised methods require costly clinical labels, and invasive and non-invasive signals differ substantially, preventing a unified method.
The paper proposes MBrain, a self-supervised framework designed to pre-train both SEEG and EEG data by learning cross-channel spatial and temporal correlations.

The framework uses graph-based multi-channel CPC for spatial correlation, instantaneous and delayed time-shift prediction for temporal correlation, and replace-discriminative learning to preserve channel characteristics.
Seizure-detection experiments on real-world EEG and SEEG datasets are reported to outperform several comparison models and indicate clinical deployment potential.

source_observation.claim: A unified self-supervised representation can be designed around shared spatial and temporal structure across heterogeneous brain-signal channels.

interpretation.claim: When measurement modalities differ, modeling relationships among channels may provide a common representation space.

application.claim: This pattern may be applicable to other multichannel physiological time-series problems with limited labels and heterogeneous sensing methods.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the approach transfers beyond EEG and SEEG or across tasks other than seizure detection.

unknowns: Dataset identities, sizes, preprocessing, and evaluation metrics are not specified.
Comparison-model identities and quantitative performance results are not specified.
The theoretical assumptions and proof details are not provided.
Clinical deployment conditions and validation procedures are not described.
